title: Singing together in the Bhakti tradition
body: Between the 11th and 17th centuries, the Bhakti tradition spread across the subcontinent through devotional hymns composed in local languages. Saints such as Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and Guru Nanak used community singing, or sankirtan, to bridge social divides. These gatherings drew large crowds and created a shared sense of community and collective emotion among devotees from many backgrounds. In some instances, singing together also became an act of defiance. In Bengal, for example, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu led public sankirtan to protest against restrictions imposed by a Qazi on devotional practices. In Assam, Sankardev composed the Kirtana Ghosha, which remains central to Vaishnava traditions today. Because Bhakti flourished through local songs and community participation (satsang), it reached wider sections of society and became more difficult to suppress.
